ZFTRAF1 (formerly C15orf39) was reported around 2023 in a multi-family study describing bi-allelic loss-of-function variants in consanguineous families (largely of Middle Eastern/South Asian origin) causing a neurodevelopmental disorder with global developmental delay, intellectual disability, hypotonia, microcephaly, and seizures. That report included several independent probands/families with segregation data and supporting functional/expression work, which meets criteria for a strong, replicated human causal association. However, the gene is relatively newly described and independent replication beyond the initial cohort collaboration is still limited, so some probability remains on "Existing." Purely biological/animal-model-only evidence (Hypothesized) or absence of any link (Novel) are unlikely given the published human genetic data.

ATP6V1C1 encodes the C1 subunit of the vacuolar H+-ATPase, a complex whose other subunits (ATP6V1A, ATP6V1B2, ATP6V0A1, ATP6V0C, ATP6V1E1, ATP6V0A2) are firmly established causes of developmental and epileptic encephalopathies, intellectual disability, and cutis laxa with neurodevelopmental features, giving strong biological/pathway rationale for a role in neurodevelopmental disorder. However, ATP6V1C1 itself has been studied mainly in osteoclast biology and cancer, and I am not aware of a well-replicated set of human probands with pathogenic ATP6V1C1 variants causing NDD, so "Established" is unlikely. Isolated de novo or biallelic candidate variants may have appeared in large developmental disorder/autism sequencing cohorts or single case reports, which would support "Existing" but at limited confidence. The strongest weight therefore falls on "Hypothesized" (pathway and functional relevance without definitive human genetic proof), with a modest residual probability that no meaningful evidence exists at all.

CFAP47 (cilia and flagella associated protein 47) is an X-linked gene whose established human disease association is with multiple morphological abnormalities of the sperm flagella (MMAF)/asthenoteratozoospermia, with additional reports linking hemizygous variants to laterality defects/heterotaxy. I am not aware of any human genetic study reporting CFAP47 variants in patients with polycystic kidney disease or renal cystic phenotypes, and it is not part of standard PKD/ciliopathy diagnostic panels (PKD1, PKD2, PKHD1, GANAB, DNAJB11, HNF1B, and NPHP-related genes). A weak conceptual link exists because CFAP47 is a ciliary/flagellar protein and PKD is a canonical ciliopathy, so a pathway-level hypothesis could be argued; however, CFAP47 functions in motile axonemes rather than the renal primary cilium, and motile ciliopathies generally do not produce cystic kidney disease. Therefore most probability falls on Novel, with a substantial minority on Hypothesized based on generic ciliary biology, and minimal weight on Existing/Established.

IRAK2 is a core component of the MyD88–IRAK4–IRAK1/2 Myddosome that drives TLR/IL-1R–dependent NF-κB activation and post-transcriptional stabilization of inflammatory transcripts, and Irak2-deficient mice show blunted cytokine production and protection in inflammatory models — a very strong biological/pathway rationale that supports "Hypothesized." Unlike IRAK4 and IRAK1 (well-established human immunodeficiency and SLE-associated loci, respectively), no recurrent Mendelian human disease caused by IRAK2 variants has been convincingly reported in multiple independent probands, so "Established" is unlikely. Some human candidate-gene/GWAS-level reports have implicated IRAK2 variants in inflammatory or infection-related phenotypes (e.g., sepsis/ARDS susceptibility, airway/asthma-related traits, occasional inclusion in inflammatory bowel or autoimmune panels), which gives modest weight to "Existing," though these are sparse and not robustly replicated. Given the clear mechanistic centrality of IRAK2 in innate immune signaling, "Novel" is improbable.

AFDN (afadin/MLLT4) encodes an adherens junction adaptor essential for cell–cell adhesion and epithelial integrity, and conditional/neural crest–specific deletion in mice produces craniofacial and palatal fusion defects, giving strong biological and animal-model plausibility for a role in orofacial clefting. Human genetic evidence is much weaker: biallelic AFDN variants are best characterized in intellectual disability/neurodevelopmental phenotypes rather than clefting, and I am not aware of robust, replicated human association or causal variant data specifically for cleft lip/palate. Some candidate-gene/exome or 6q27 deletion reports may include cleft-related craniofacial features, which could support a limited "Existing" designation, but such evidence is sparse and not definitive. Therefore the weight falls predominantly on Hypothesized, with a moderate allowance for Existing and little support for Established.

KAT2B (PCAF) is a lysine acetyltransferase involved in chromatin remodeling and transcriptional coactivation, but it is not among the recognized monogenic causes of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (e.g., NPHS1, NPHS2, WT1, PLCE1, INF2, ACTN4, TRPC6, COQ-pathway and nucleoporin genes). I am not aware of replicated human genetic studies reporting pathogenic KAT2B variants in SRNS probands or families, so "Established" is very unlikely. There is plausible biological relevance—histone acetylation/deacetylation and KAT2B/GCN5 activity have been implicated in podocyte injury, TGF-β signaling and glomerular disease models (largely rodent and in vitro), which supports a "Hypothesized" relationship. A small residual probability is assigned to "Existing" in case KAT2B has appeared as a novel candidate gene in an exome/whole-genome sequencing cohort of nephrotic syndrome that I am not recalling, but incidental co-mention remains at least as likely.

MMS19 encodes a core component of the cytosolic iron–sulfur cluster assembly (CIA) targeting complex, and defective Fe–S cluster biogenesis is a well-established mechanism in neurodegeneration (e.g., frataxin/Friedreich ataxia, NUBPL, NFU1, BOLA3), giving a strong biological/pathway rationale that supports "Hypothesized." Functional work (Stehling et al.) shows MMS19 loss impairs maturation of Fe–S proteins involved in DNA repair, iron homeostasis, and mitochondrial function, but most of this is cell-based or model-organism data rather than patient genetics. I have some recollection of isolated case-level reports of biallelic MMS19 variants in patients with a multisystem/neurodevelopmental phenotype with regression, which if confirmed would justify "Existing," but this evidence is sparse and not clearly replicated in classical neurodegenerative disease. There is no robust, replicated human genetic evidence establishing MMS19 as a cause of neurodegenerative disease, so "Established" receives minimal weight. A small residual is left for "Novel" in case the human genetic reports do not exist or are unrelated to neurodegeneration.

CNKSR1 encodes a multidomain scaffold (CNK1) for Ras/MAPK and Rho signaling, pathways central to RASopathies and synaptic development, and its paralog CNKSR2 is a well-established cause of X-linked intellectual disability/Houge-type syndrome with epilepsy — giving strong biological plausibility that supports a "Hypothesized" relationship. However, I am not aware of replicated, well-curated human genetic evidence (e.g., recurrent de novo variants in large NDD exome cohorts, ClinGen gene–disease validity classification) implicating CNKSR1 itself in neurodevelopmental disorder, so "Established" is very unlikely. There may be isolated candidate-variant reports or inclusion in 1p36.11 CNV/exome candidate lists, which would justify some weight for "Existing," but such evidence would be limited and not definitive. A residual possibility remains that CNKSR1 is only incidentally co-mentioned with NDD through paralog analogy, keeping some weight on "Novel."

COQ5 encodes a C-methyltransferase in the coenzyme Q10 biosynthetic pathway, and other COQ genes (COQ2, COQ4, COQ8A/ADCK3, COQ9, PDSS1/2) are well-established causes of primary CoQ10 deficiency with encephalopathy, developmental delay, and ataxia, giving strong biological plausibility. For COQ5 specifically, I recall a single human report (Malicdan et al., Human Mutation 2018) describing siblings from one family with a 3'UTR duplication causing reduced COQ5 protein, presenting with cerebellar ataxia, intellectual disability/developmental delay, and static encephalomyopathy, with supportive functional and yeast complementation data. This constitutes credible but limited, largely unreplicated human genetic evidence, best fitting "Existing" rather than "Established," since replication in independent probands is sparse. Some probability remains for "Established" if additional families have since been reported, and for "Hypothesized" given that much of the supporting mechanistic work is in yeast/cell models.

MRPS23 encodes a small subunit mitochondrial ribosomal protein, and biallelic variants have been reported in humans with combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency (OMIM 618952, COXPD46), notably a patient with hepatic disease and multiple respiratory chain complex deficiencies described by Kohda et al. (2016), with supporting functional/complementation data. However, the number of independent probands/families reported is very small (essentially one to a few), so replication across multiple independent clinical studies is limited, which is why curation efforts have typically rated this gene–disease relationship as limited/moderate rather than definitive. This places most weight on "Existing," with meaningful residual probability that additional cases published since have elevated it toward "Established." The clear biological relevance of mitoribosomal subunits to OXPHOS deficiency also supports a small "Hypothesized" allocation, while "Novel" is nearly excluded since the disease entity was defined by this gene.

DDX59 biallelic variants were first linked to orofaciodigital syndrome (OFD type V / Váradi-Papp-like phenotype) by Shamseldin et al. (2013) in a consanguineous family, with supporting functional work showing that DDX59 depletion impairs ciliogenesis and Sonic hedgehog signaling; Salpietro et al. and subsequent case reports described additional independent patients with ECO/OFD-spectrum features. OFD syndromes are canonically classified as ciliopathies, so the phenotype maps directly onto the queried disease category. However, the total number of reported human families remains small and gene–disease validity has generally been curated as limited-to-moderate rather than definitive, and some authors question whether DDX59 acts through a strictly ciliary mechanism. Points are therefore split roughly evenly between Established and Existing, with a small residual for a purely biology-based (Hypothesized) interpretation.

PRICKLE2 (a planar cell polarity gene at 3p14.1) has human genetic evidence linking it to neurodevelopmental phenotypes: Sowers et al. (2013, Molecular Psychiatry) reported rare missense variants and a deletion disrupting PRICKLE2 in patients with autism spectrum disorder, supported by Prickle2-knockout mouse behavioral and synaptic phenotypes; Tao et al. (2011, AJHG) implicated PRICKLE2 variants in myoclonic epilepsy, and 3p14 deletions involving PRICKLE2 have been described in patients with developmental delay, intellectual disability, seizures, and autistic features. These reports are credible human findings but involve small numbers of probands, incomplete segregation/penetrance data, and limited independent replication, so the gene is not firmly established as a definitive cause of a complex neurodevelopmental disorder. Much of the mechanistic support (synaptic PSD-95/NMDA receptor interactions, Wnt/PCP signaling, mouse behavior) is non-human, which supports but does not upgrade the human evidence. Therefore the weight falls mainly on "Existing," with a moderate share for "Established" and a meaningful share for "Hypothesized."

WBP2 is listed as the gene for DFNB107, autosomal recessive nonsyndromic hearing loss, based principally on a single 2016 study (Buniello et al., EMBO Mol Med) that combined a Wbp2-null mouse model showing progressive hearing loss and abnormal cochlear glutamatergic synapses with the identification of homozygous WBP2 variants in two consanguineous human families with childhood-onset progressive deafness. This provides credible human genetic evidence, but it comes from one report with few probands and has not been robustly replicated in independent cohorts; gene-curation efforts have generally rated the evidence as limited rather than definitive. Therefore "Existing" is the most probable category, with some residual probability for "Established" (should later families/reports exist) and for "Hypothesized" (if the human evidence is judged insufficient and only the mouse/functional cochlear data are counted). "Novel" is very unlikely given the explicit OMIM DFNB107 designation.

ZBTB40 is best characterized as a 1p36 bone mineral density GWAS locus and, more recently, as a cause of recessive osteogenesis imperfecta–like skeletal disease, not as a neurodevelopmental disorder gene. I am not aware of any replicated clinical cohort establishing that ZBTB40 variants cause intellectual disability, autism, or global developmental delay, so "Established" is very unlikely. Some weak support could come from sporadic de novo variants reported in large exome/sequencing studies of developmental disorders or autism, and from its location within/near the 1p36 deletion region associated with developmental delay, which would justify limited "Existing" weight. Its biology as a BTB-zinc finger transcription factor with broad expression, including brain, provides a plausible but unproven mechanistic rationale, supporting "Hypothesized." Overall the evidence base is thin, so substantial probability remains that any co-mention is incidental ("Novel").

phenotype: hypogonadotropic hypogonadism 21 with or without anosmia
justification: FLRT3 was designated HH21 in OMIM based on Miraoui et al. (2013, AJHG), which reported rare heterozygous missense variants in FLRT3 among patients with congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism/Kallmann syndrome, framed as part of the FGF8/FGFR1 signaling network (alongside FGF17, IL17RD, DUSP6, SPRY4). This provides credible human genetic evidence, but the variants were mostly heterozygous, frequently in an oligogenic context, with limited segregation data and little independent replication in subsequent CHH cohorts; some gene-curation efforts classify FLRT3 as limited/disputed. Supporting biology (FLRT3 as an FGFR1-interacting protein and its role in FGF signaling and neuronal/axon guidance) strengthens plausibility but is largely functional/in vitro. Therefore "Existing" is most appropriate, with modest weight to "Established" (given OMIM phenotype designation) and to "Hypothesized" (if the human variant evidence is judged insufficient).

SLC4A8 (NDCBE) is a neuronally expressed sodium-driven chloride/bicarbonate exchanger that regulates intracellular and synaptic pH, neuronal excitability, and GABA-A/glutamatergic signaling, and knockout mice show altered excitability and affective/behavioral phenotypes — this biology provides a plausible but indirect rationale for a role in psychosis, favoring "Hypothesized." I am not aware of a genome-wide significant schizophrenia GWAS locus at SLC4A8; the well-replicated schizophrenia solute-carrier hit is SLC39A8 (A391T), which is frequently confused with SLC4A8. Some candidate-gene, rare-variant, CNV, or brain-expression studies may have listed SLC4A8 among suggestive findings, so a modest probability is given to "Existing," but such reports would be limited and unreplicated. There is essentially no basis for "Established." A substantial share remains on "Novel" because the gene may only appear incidentally in large screens without any specific human genetic evidence.

USP27X was identified as a candidate X-linked intellectual disability gene in the large X-exome sequencing study of unresolved ID families (Hu et al., Mol Psychiatry 2016), which reported a truncating variant segregating in an affected family, and it has an OMIM entry for X-linked intellectual developmental disorder (MRX105). This constitutes credible human genetic evidence, but the number of independently reported probands/families remains small and replication is sparse, so most curation efforts would classify the evidence as limited rather than definitive. Supporting biology (deubiquitinase acting on substrates such as MCL1 and involvement in neuronal/ubiquitin-proteasome pathways) adds plausibility but is secondary to the human data. Therefore the weight falls mainly on "Existing," with a meaningful minority chance that accumulated case reports now justify "Established," and little support for "Novel."

TNK2 (ACK1) is a non-receptor tyrosine kinase that has been implicated in human epilepsy through a report of biallelic/de novo TNK2 variants in severe infantile-onset epilepsy (Hitomi et al., Ann Neurol 2013), with supporting functional data on synaptic/dendritic signaling; it is consequently included on some epilepsy gene panels. However, that phenotype is an early-onset epileptic encephalopathy rather than classic genetic generalized (idiopathic generalized) epilepsy, and I am not aware of replicated GGE-specific association from case–control cohorts or GWAS. Thus there is at least one credible human genetic report linking TNK2 to epilepsy broadly, which supports "Existing" for a related epilepsy phenotype, but the link to GGE specifically is indirect. Substantial weight also goes to "Hypothesized," since much of the mechanistic support is functional/in vitro and pathway-based, and some weight to "Novel" because GGE proper may have no TNK2 evidence at all. Evidence is clearly insufficient for "Established."

There is credible human genetic evidence linking SIRT1 to autoimmunity, most notably the report of a rare SIRT1 missense variant (Leu107Pro) segregating with autoimmune type 1 diabetes in a Dutch family (Biason-Lauber et al., Cell Metabolism 2013), plus candidate-gene association studies of SIRT1 polymorphisms (e.g., rs3758391, rs7895833) with multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, Behçet's disease, and autoimmune thyroid disease in various populations. These findings are generally single-study, modest in size, and inconsistently replicated, and SIRT1 is not a robust genome-wide significant locus for major autoimmune diseases, so "Established" is unlikely. Substantial supporting biology exists independent of genetics—SIRT1 deacetylates FoxP3, RORγt, and NF-κB, regulating Treg/Th17 balance, and Sirt1-deficient mice develop lupus-like autoimmunity and reduced SIRT1 expression is seen in SLE and RA patients—which would place it at least in "Hypothesized" if the human genetic reports were discounted. Weighting accordingly, "Existing" is the most probable category with meaningful residual probability for "Hypothesized."

phenotype: neurodevelopmental disorder with cerebellar hypoplasia and spasticity
justification: INTS8 is listed in OMIM as the cause of "neurodevelopmental disorder with cerebellar hypoplasia and spasticity" (NEDCHS), based primarily on Oegema et al. (2017, PLoS Genetics), which reported biallelic INTS8 variants in affected human siblings with severe developmental delay, cerebellar hypoplasia/atrophy, and spasticity, alongside INTS1 variants in a related Integrator-complex phenotype. That work included human patient genetics plus functional support (impaired snRNA 3′-end processing, disrupted Integrator complex assembly), making the causal link credible. However, the number of independent probands/families is small and replication in additional unrelated families has been limited, so the evidence sits at the boundary between definitive and limited (ClinGen-style "moderate/limited"). Purely hypothesized or novel classifications are unlikely given direct human variant evidence with matching phenotype.

MYBPC3 is definitively established as a cause of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (and biallelic truncating variants cause severe neonatal/infantile cardiomyopathy and left ventricular non-compaction), but these are cardiomyopathies rather than structural congenital heart disease per se. Human evidence linking MYBPC3 to structural CHD is more limited: rare/de novo and inherited MYBPC3 variants have been reported in CHD cohorts (e.g., sarcomere-gene screens, exome studies of CHD probands, LVNC co-occurring with septal defects or Ebstein-like anomalies), though sarcomere genes such as MYH6 and MYH7 carry far stronger CHD evidence. Because MYBPC3 causes congenital-onset cardiac disease and non-compaction phenotypes that overlap with recognized CHD spectrum, "Existing" is the most defensible category, with genuine support also for a purely biological/hypothesized link via sarcomere function in cardiac development. Established is unlikely given no replicated demonstration that MYBPC3 variants cause structural malformations across independent probands, and Novel is improbable given repeated human co-occurrence reports.

phenotype: epilepsy, early-onset, with or without developmental delay
justification: SETD1A is an OMIM-recognized disease gene, and "Epilepsy, early-onset, with or without developmental delay" (MIM 618832) is attributed to heterozygous de novo/loss-of-function SETD1A variants, based on a cohort report of multiple unrelated probands with early-onset seizures. Additional human evidence comes from broader SETD1A neurodevelopmental disorder cohorts (e.g., Kummeling et al., 2021) in which a substantial subset of individuals have epilepsy, as well as large de novo variant studies in developmental disorders and schizophrenia. This constitutes replicated human genetic evidence supporting causality, favoring "Established." Some residual uncertainty remains because much of the epilepsy-specific evidence stems from a limited number of cohorts and the phenotype is variably penetrant within the broader SETD1A neurodevelopmental spectrum, which is why meaningful weight is retained for "Existing."

Biallelic CLPB variants are well established as causing 3-methylglutaconic aciduria type VII with cataracts, neurologic involvement and neutropenia (MEGCANN), and monoallelic variants cause severe congenital neutropenia; however, the classic neuroimaging phenotype is brain atrophy, delayed myelination and corpus callosum abnormalities rather than the symmetric basal ganglia/brainstem lesions defining Leigh syndrome. CLPB is not typically included in curated Leigh syndrome gene panels or major Leigh syndrome cohort studies, so replicated human evidence for a causal Leigh phenotype is lacking. Nonetheless, CLPB encodes a mitochondrial intermembrane-space disaggregase, and its deficiency produces a mitochondrial encephalopathy with 3-MGA-uria, making the biology directly relevant and Leigh-like presentations plausible; isolated case reports describing Leigh-like MRI features cannot be excluded. I therefore weight Hypothesized most heavily, with meaningful probability for Existing (a single or few human case reports) and residual weight for Novel, and minimal weight for Established.

IARS2 encodes the mitochondrial isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase, and biallelic variants are well established as causing a multisystem mitochondrial disorder, most classically CAGSSS syndrome (cataracts, growth hormone deficiency, sensory neuropathy, sensorineural hearing loss, skeletal dysplasia), with additional reported phenotypes including sideroblastic anemia and infantile encephalopathy. Several human case reports specifically describe Leigh or Leigh-like syndrome with characteristic basal ganglia/brainstem MRI lesions in patients with biallelic IARS2 variants (e.g., Japanese siblings reported with CAGSSS, Leigh and West syndrome, and additional isolated Leigh-syndrome probands), which supports at least the "Existing" level and arguably "Established." However, the number of independent Leigh-syndrome probands is relatively small compared with the broader IARS2 phenotype, so replication for this specific phenotype is limited. Mechanistically, defects in mitochondrial aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases are a recognized and common cause of Leigh syndrome through impaired mitochondrial translation and OXPHOS deficiency, making the biological link highly plausible. I therefore weight Existing highest, with substantial probability on Established and little on Hypothesized or Novel.

Well-supported Tourette syndrome candidate genes from human studies include SLITRK1, HDC, CELSR3, WWC1, NRXN1, CNTNAP2, AADAC, IMMP2L, and the FLT3 locus from GWAS; HNRNPA0 is not among the recognized or replicated candidates. I am not aware of any linkage, GWAS, CNV, or de novo variant study specifically implicating HNRNPA0 in Tourette syndrome or in tic disorders. HNRNPA0 encodes a broadly expressed hnRNP involved in mRNA stability and stress-response (MK2/p38) signaling, and other hnRNP family members (e.g., HNRNPU, HNRNPH2) are linked to neurodevelopmental phenotypes, which provides only a weak, generic biological rationale that could support a "hypothesized" classification. Any appearance of HNRNPA0 in TS literature would most likely be incidental (e.g., within a large CNV region or an unreplicated exome hit). Therefore most probability mass falls on Novel, with a moderate allocation to Hypothesized and a small allowance for an obscure single-study human association.

ITSN1 lies in the chromosome 21q22 region implicated in Down syndrome and encodes a scaffold protein central to clathrin-mediated synaptic vesicle endocytosis and Cdc42/Ras GEF signaling in neurons, providing strong biological plausibility (and mouse knockouts show learning and behavioral deficits), which supports the Hypothesized tier. Beyond biology, human genetic data exist: rare protein-truncating and de novo variants in ITSN1 have been reported in autism/developmental disorder exome cohorts and the gene is highly loss-of-function intolerant, and 21q22.11 microdeletions encompassing ITSN1 have been described in patients with developmental delay. Large-scale burden analyses (e.g., UK Biobank/Genomics England work linking ITSN1 PTVs to Parkinson's disease) also cite prior associations of ITSN1 haploinsufficiency with neurodevelopmental phenotypes. However, ITSN1 has not reached genome-wide/definitive gene-level significance as a standalone NDD gene in the largest ASD/DD consortia analyses, and replication in independent well-phenotyped probands is limited, so full "Established" status is not clearly met. The weight therefore falls mostly on "Existing," with meaningful residual probability for "Established" and "Hypothesized."

ILK (integrin-linked kinase) is a core component of the cardiomyocyte costamere/focal adhesion complex, a pathway repeatedly implicated in dilated cardiomyopathy, and zebrafish (main squeeze) and cardiac-specific knockout mouse models develop dilated cardiomyopathy—strong biological/animal support. Human genetic evidence exists primarily from Knöll et al. (Circulation 2007), which reported rare ILK missense variants (e.g., A262V, P70L) in DCM patients alongside LAMA4 variants, with functional zebrafish rescue experiments. However, this evidence rests largely on a single report with few probands and limited independent replication or segregation data, and gene-curation efforts have generally rated ILK–DCM as limited/disputed rather than definitive. Therefore "Existing" is the most likely category, with substantial residual probability on "Hypothesized" if the human variant evidence is judged insufficient and the case rests mainly on model organisms.

phenotype: short stature and microcephaly with genital anomalies
justification: CENPT encodes a constitutive centromere-associated network (CCAN) kinetochore component, and several centromere/kinetochore genes (CENPE, CENPJ, CENPF) are established causes of microcephalic growth-restriction syndromes, making the biology highly plausible. I recall a specific human report of biallelic CENPT variants in a consanguineous family with short stature, microcephaly and genital/gonadal anomalies, which corresponds to a named OMIM phenotype, supporting at least "Existing" level human genetic evidence. However, to my knowledge the evidence rests on very few probands/families with limited independent replication, so a fully "Established" classification is uncertain. Some weight remains for "Hypothesized" in case the human data are largely supported by functional/cellular experiments rather than multiple independent clinical cohorts, and a small residual probability for "Novel" if I am conflating CENPT with another CENP-family gene.

HKDC1 (hexokinase domain containing 1) is primarily characterized in glucose metabolism, gestational diabetes, hepatic glucose handling, and more recently cancer metabolism; I am not aware of any human genetic study implicating HKDC1 variants in retinitis pigmentosa or other inherited retinal dystrophies. It is not listed among RetNet retinal disease genes. The main plausible link is indirect: its close paralog HK1 harbors a recurrent p.Glu847Lys variant causing autosomal dominant RP (RP79), which could motivate hypotheses that hexokinase-family dysfunction, photoreceptor glucose metabolism, or HKDC1 expression in retina contributes to degeneration, but such reasoning is largely speculative and not supported by dedicated functional or model studies of HKDC1 in retina. Therefore most weight falls on Novel, with a meaningful minority on Hypothesized due to pathway/paralog biology, and only small probabilities for Existing or Established in case of an obscure candidate-gene or exome report I am unaware of.

SERPINA11 is a poorly characterized member of the SERPINA gene cluster on 14q32.1 with no established human disease phenotype and no OMIM disease entry. Known monogenic causes of non-immune hydrops fetalis include alpha-thalassemia (HBA1/HBA2), lysosomal storage disorders, RASopathies, lymphatic development genes (e.g., PIEZO1, EPHB4, RASA1), and cardiac/metabolic genes—SERPINA11 is not among reported candidates in the large exome/genome sequencing cohorts of hydrops. Some serpins have plausible relevance to coagulation, complement, or vascular/lymphatic biology, which leaves a small margin for a purely biological/hypothetical link, and SERPINA11 could conceivably appear as an incidental variant in a fetal sequencing study, but I am not aware of any credible human genetic report. The evidence therefore overwhelmingly supports a Novel classification, with a modest allowance for hypothesized pathway-level plausibility.

I recall a human genetic study (International Journal of Oral Science, ~2022) reporting a novel heterozygous variant in ZNF862 segregating with hereditary gingival fibromatosis in a Chinese family, supported by functional experiments in gingival fibroblasts showing effects on proliferation and extracellular matrix/collagen pathways. This constitutes credible human genetic evidence, but to my knowledge it derives essentially from a single family/report without broad independent replication across multiple unrelated probands, unlike SOS1 (GINGF1) or the more recently reported REST variants. Therefore the evidence best fits "Existing," with some probability that additional confirmatory families have since been published, which would push it toward "Established." A small residual probability is assigned to purely biological/functional support only, and minimal probability to no evidence at all.

IFT74 encodes an intraflagellar transport-B core component essential for flagellar/ciliary assembly, and it is a recognized disease gene for Bardet-Biedl syndrome and short-rib thoracic dysplasia. For male infertility, Lorès and colleagues reported a homozygous missense (and related) IFT74 variant in an infertile man with asthenozoospermia/abnormal flagella without syndromic ciliopathy features, supported by functional and model-organism data, and this underlies the OMIM designation spermatogenic failure 58. The human genetic evidence is credible but derives from a small number of probands with limited independent replication, favoring "Existing" over "Established." Some weight remains for "Established" in case additional cohorts (e.g., Chinese asthenoteratozoospermia series) have replicated bi-allelic IFT74 variants, and a small residual weight for "Hypothesized" if much of the support is animal/in vitro.

NEBL encodes nebulette, a cardiac Z-disc/thin-filament anchoring protein, giving strong biological plausibility for dilated cardiomyopathy. Purevjav et al. (JACC 2010) reported rare missense variants (e.g., K60N, Q128R, G202R, A592E) in human DCM probands, supported by transgenic mouse models recapitulating DCM, and subsequent case reports have linked NEBL to pediatric DCM/left ventricular noncompaction. However, replication in independent large cohorts has been weak, segregation data are sparse, and formal ClinGen gene–disease curation for DCM has downgraded NEBL to limited/disputed status, with much of the supporting evidence being murine or in vitro. Therefore the human genetic evidence best fits "Existing" rather than "Established," with substantial residual weight on "Hypothesized" because much of the causal support is model-organism/functional rather than definitive human variant data.

GATC encodes a subunit of the mitochondrial glutamyl-tRNA(Gln) amidotransferase (GatCAB) complex, essential for mitochondrial translation, so its biology is directly relevant to oxidative phosphorylation disorders. Human genetic evidence exists: Friederich et al. (2018) reported biallelic pathogenic variants in QRSL1, GATB, and GATC in patients with lethal infantile mitochondrial cardiomyopathy/combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency, with functional validation (reduced OXPHOS complexes, rescue experiments). GATC is recognized in OMIM as the gene for combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 42, supporting an established causal role. However, the number of independent GATC probands is small compared with QRSL1/GATB, so some curation frameworks might classify the evidence as moderate/limited rather than definitive, justifying substantial weight on "Existing."

ATG9A is a core autophagy machinery protein with well-documented roles in innate immunity, including trafficking of STING from the ER/Golgi and regulation of cGAS–STING type I interferon signaling, inflammasome control, xenophagy of intracellular bacteria, and antigen presentation — providing a strong biological rationale linking it to immune function. However, the human genetic disease associations reported for ATG9A to date are primarily biallelic variants in neurodevelopmental phenotypes (developmental delay, hypotonia, brain malformations), not a defined inborn error of immunity. Most immune-related evidence derives from cell lines, knockout/knockdown systems, and mouse models rather than patients with immunodeficiency. I therefore weight "Hypothesized" heavily, allow a modest probability that an isolated case report or immunophenotyping study in a patient exists ("Existing"), and retain some probability that co-mentions are incidental ("Novel"). Established causation in independent human probands with immunodeficiency is very unlikely.

CALCRL is the gene assigned to lymphatic malformation 8 (LMPHM8, autosomal recessive nonimmune hydrops fetalis with lymphatic dysplasia) in OMIM, based principally on a single consanguineous family reported by Mackie et al. (J Exp Med, 2018) in which a homozygous hypomorphic variant affecting the translation start codon segregated with recurrent fetal hydrops and lymphatic dysplasia. This human genetic finding was supported by strong functional work and by Calcrl/Ramp2/adrenomedullin-pathway knockout mice, which show lymphatic hypoplasia and hydrops, making the biology highly relevant. However, replication in independent probands or families is sparse, so the evidence is credible but not definitive—consistent with "Existing" (limited/moderate) rather than "Established." A modest allocation to Established reflects the multiple affected individuals within the reported family and the compelling functional support, while Hypothesized retains some weight because much of the mechanistic proof derives from mouse and in vitro models.

HIVEP1 (Schnurri-1, ZAS1) is best known from human GWAS for venous thromboembolism, not neurodevelopmental phenotypes. Its paralog HIVEP2 (Schnurri-2) is a well-established cause of intellectual disability/developmental delay with de novo loss-of-function variants, which makes HIVEP1 a strong biological candidate through shared NF-κB/BMP-signaling transcriptional regulation and brain expression; this supports a "Hypothesized" weighting. There may be scattered candidate variants reported in large exome/CNV cohorts (e.g., de novo variants in DD/ASD trio studies or 6p24 deletions), but I am not aware of replicated, statistically robust human evidence establishing HIVEP1 as a bona fide NDD gene. Therefore most probability sits in Hypothesized, with meaningful mass for Existing (isolated human case-level reports) and some for Novel if no human variant evidence exists, and very little for Established.

VEZF1 (ZNF161) is a zinc-finger transcription factor best characterized in vascular/endothelial development, regulating targets such as endothelin-1 and IL-3, with knockout mice showing embryonic vascular remodeling defects — biology that is cardiovascular-relevant but not specifically tied to myocardial dilatation. I am not aware of replicated human genetic studies, families, or curated gene–disease validity assessments (e.g., ClinGen/GenCC DCM panels) that list VEZF1 as a dilated cardiomyopathy gene; standard DCM gene panels do not include it. At most, VEZF1 might appear as a candidate from a single exome/CNV or GWAS-adjacent report or as a modifier in cardiac transcriptional networks, which would only support "Existing" weakly. Because the strongest supporting data are animal/in vitro and pathway-level rather than human variant-based, most weight belongs in Hypothesized, with substantial probability that any co-mention is incidental (Novel).

RAB35 is a small GTPase with strong neurobiological relevance: it regulates endosomal recycling, cytokinesis, exosome release, and neurite outgrowth/neuronal polarity (via ACAP2, MICAL-L1, DENND1/connecdenn GEFs), and is highly expressed in brain, with rodent and cell models showing effects on neurite extension and synaptic protein trafficking. Several related Rab-family genes (RAB11A/B, RAB39B, RAB18, RAB3GAP1/2) are established neurodevelopmental disease genes, providing pathway-level support but not direct evidence for RAB35. My recollection of human genetic data for RAB35 is limited—there may be isolated de novo or candidate variants reported in developmental delay/intellectual disability cohorts or large exome/denovo-enrichment datasets, but I am not aware of a replicated, well-curated gene–disease validation. Therefore the biology-based "Hypothesized" category is most probable, with meaningful weight on "Existing" if a single small human report exists, and low weight on "Established."

The existence of a numbered OMIM phenotype "retinitis pigmentosa 92" tied to HKDC1 implies that at least one human genetic study reported (likely biallelic) HKDC1 variants segregating with non-syndromic RP, which satisfies the "Existing" threshold. My recollection is that this designation rests on a small number of recent reports (a few consanguineous or otherwise limited families), possibly with supporting functional or model-organism data, rather than broad independent replication across many cohorts. HKDC1 is primarily known for hexokinase activity and glucose metabolism (e.g., gestational diabetes associations), so photoreceptor-relevant metabolic biology provides a plausible mechanism but is largely supportive rather than definitive. Therefore most weight goes to "Existing," with meaningful probability on "Established" if independent families have since been published, a smaller share to "Hypothesized" if the human variant evidence is weaker than the OMIM designation suggests, and minimal weight to "Novel."

STK33 encodes a testis-enriched serine/threonine kinase required for sperm flagellar development and motility; Stk33-null mice and knockout non-human primates are infertile with asthenoteratozoospermia, and STK33 has been pursued as a reversible male contraceptive target (e.g., inhibitor CDD-2807). Importantly, the existence of a dedicated OMIM entry (spermatogenic failure 93) implies at least one human report of biallelic loss-of-function/missense STK33 variants in infertile men with oligo-astheno-teratozoospermia, supported by functional modeling. Because such human genetic evidence appears to derive from a small number of probands/families with limited independent replication, "Existing" is most likely, with substantial probability that multiple independent human reports now justify "Established." Purely hypothesized status is unlikely given human variant data, and "Novel" is essentially excluded by the strong, direct spermatogenesis biology.

SLC51A encodes OSTα, which heterodimerizes with OSTβ (SLC51B) to mediate basolateral bile acid efflux from enterocytes and hepatocytes, making it mechanistically central to bile acid handling and cholestasis. Human evidence exists: biallelic SLC51A variants were reported in patients with congenital chronic diarrhea, cholestasis, and liver fibrosis (e.g., Gao et al., Hepatology 2020), paralleling the earlier SLC51B/OSTβ deficiency cases; this places SLC51A within the PFIC gene family (typically catalogued as a distinct PFIC subtype rather than PFIC6, which is usually attributed to MYO5B). Because the human reports involve only one or very few probands and the exact numbered PFIC designation may not match, the evidence is credible but limited rather than replicated and definitive. Strong supporting functional/mouse data (Ostα-null mice with altered bile acid homeostasis) also justify some weight on Hypothesized, while Novel is unlikely given the clear biological and clinical link.

TRIM47 lies within the chromosome 17q25.1 locus (TRIM47/TRIM65/WBP2/UNC13D region) that is among the most robustly replicated GWAS signals for white matter hyperintensity burden, a canonical MRI marker of cerebral small vessel disease, with replication across multiple human cohorts (CHARGE, UK Biobank, stroke consortia) and links to lacunar stroke. These are human genetic association data for common variants and for a precursor/subtype phenotype rather than proof that TRIM47 mutations cause a Mendelian small vessel disease, which best fits "Existing." Supporting mechanistic work—endothelial-enriched TRIM47 expression, blood–brain barrier dysfunction and white matter changes in Trim47-deficient mice, and eQTL/fine-mapping nominating TRIM47 as the causal gene at the locus—strengthens biological plausibility but is largely non-human, so some weight goes to "Hypothesized." A small probability is retained for "Established" because of the breadth of replication and convergent functional validation, and "Novel" is essentially excluded.

NRG1 (neuregulin-1) type III is one of the best-characterized axonal signals controlling Schwann cell development, myelination, myelin sheath thickness, remyelination, and nerve regeneration via ErbB2/ErbB3 receptors, making its biology directly and strongly relevant to peripheral neuropathy — but this evidence comes overwhelmingly from mouse models and in vitro work, which supports "Hypothesized." In humans, NRG1 sequence variants are well known in schizophrenia and Hirschsprung disease, not as a Mendelian cause of hereditary neuropathy; NRG1 is not listed among CMT/inherited neuropathy genes in clinical gene panels. There is limited human work measuring soluble/serum NRG1 levels as a biomarker or candidate modifier in CMT1A and diabetic neuropathy, and some candidate-gene/expression studies, which could provide weak "Existing" support, though these are expression rather than clear variant-based association. No replicated human genetic studies demonstrate causality, so "Established" is very unlikely. "Novel" is also unlikely given the extensive mechanistic literature tying NRG1 to peripheral nerve myelination and injury responses.

GTF3A encodes TFIIIA, a general transcription factor required for RNA polymerase III–mediated transcription; Pol III is a well-described cytosolic sensor of AT-rich viral DNA (including HSV-1) that generates 5'-triphosphate RNA ligands for RIG-I and type I IFN induction, a pathway central to the forebrain-specific antiviral immunity implicated in herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE). Human inborn errors in related Pol III components (POLR3A, POLR3C, POLR3E, POLR3F) and other Pol III–linked genes (e.g., SNORA31, DBR1) have been reported in severe herpesvirus disease and HSE, giving GTF3A strong biological/pathway plausibility. However, I am not aware of robust, replicated human genetic evidence that GTF3A variants cause HSE, and any candidate reports would be single-patient or preliminary at best. Therefore the weight falls mainly on "Hypothesized," with some probability that a single human case/cohort report exists ("Existing"), and a lesser chance the pair is essentially unreported ("Novel").

NPTX1 (neuronal pentraxin 1) has been reported in the human genetics literature as a candidate cause of autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia, notably in a study describing heterozygous NPTX1 variants segregating in family/families with late-onset ADCA, supported by functional work implicating endoplasmic reticulum stress and impaired protein secretion. This constitutes credible human genetic evidence, but the number of independent probands/families is small and independent replication in other cohorts is limited, so the association falls short of firmly established gene–disease validity. The strong cerebellar/synaptic expression and neuronal pentraxin biology also provide plausible mechanistic support, which would place it at least in the hypothesized tier if the human data were discounted. Accordingly, most weight goes to "Existing," with meaningful residual probability for "Established" should additional families have been reported, and small weight to purely biological or incidental categories.

MCF2L encodes DBS, a Dbl-family Rho/Cdc42 guanine nucleotide exchange factor with documented roles in endothelial cell migration and angiogenesis in cell-based and mouse studies, and RhoA/Cdc42 signaling is a core mechanism in vascular malformation biology (e.g., CCM, TIE2/PIK3CA pathways). However, the well-replicated human genetic associations for MCF2L involve osteoarthritis, tendinopathy, and neurologic traits rather than vascular anomalies. I am not aware of credible human germline or somatic variant reports implicating MCF2L as a cause of venous, arteriovenous, lymphatic, or cavernous malformations, and it is not on standard vascular anomaly gene panels. The biological plausibility via angiogenic RhoGEF signaling justifies weighting "Hypothesized" highest, with substantial residual probability for "Novel" since the gene–phenotype link may be purely incidental, and only small probability for human-variant-based Existing/Established evidence.

TLR4 missense variants D299G (rs4986790) and T399I (rs4986791) have been repeatedly tested in human case-control cohorts of Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, with several positive reports and multiple meta-analyses (e.g., Browning et al., Shen et al.) supporting a modest association, particularly in European populations. However, results are inconsistent across populations, effect sizes are small, and TLR4 has not emerged as a genome-wide significant locus in large IBD GWAS/Immunochip studies, so a definitive causal role is not established. Strong supporting biology exists (LPS sensing, NF-κB signaling, altered TLR4 expression in inflamed intestinal mucosa, and Tlr4-deficient mouse colitis models), but this alone would only justify "Hypothesized." Given credible but non-definitive human genetic association evidence, "Existing" is the most appropriate category, with some residual probability for "Established" given the volume of replicated meta-analytic data.

phenotype: congenital anomaly of kidney and urinary tract
justification: SIX2 encodes a master transcription factor of cap mesenchyme nephron progenitors, and Six2-null mice show premature progenitor depletion with severe renal hypoplasia, providing very strong biological/animal support. In humans, Weber et al. (JASN 2008) reported rare heterozygous SIX2 variants in patients with renal hypodysplasia/CAKUT alongside BMP4, and subsequent case reports and CAKUT cohort sequencing have occasionally implicated SIX2 (including copy-number changes), supporting at least "Existing" human evidence. However, replication is sparse, variants are often of uncertain significance with incomplete segregation, and SIX2 is not consistently included in definitive curated CAKUT gene panels, so "Established" is less likely. A residual share is left for "Hypothesized" because much of the compelling evidence remains murine/functional rather than definitive human genetic proof.

PHF10 (BAF45a) encodes a subunit of the neural progenitor-specific BAF/PBAF chromatin remodeling complex, and multiple paralogous complex members (ARID1A/B, SMARCB1, SMARCA4, SMARCE1, ARID2, DPF2/BAF45d) are well-established causes of Coffin–Siris syndrome and related BAFopathies presenting with multiple congenital anomalies and dysmorphic features, making a biologically grounded hypothesis very strong. However, I am not aware of a replicated, curated gene–disease validity assertion (e.g., ClinGen "Definitive") linking PHF10 variants to a specific MCA/dysmorphic syndrome. There may be limited human evidence in the form of candidate de novo variants in large neurodevelopmental cohorts or 6q27 deletions encompassing PHF10, which would support the "Existing" tier but is not definitive. Much of the supporting evidence (BAF45a subunit switching, mouse neural progenitor studies) is functional/animal rather than human genetic, so those points belong in "Hypothesized." A small residual probability remains that the pairing is essentially incidental.

Androgen insensitivity syndrome is a well-defined X-linked disorder caused by loss-of-function variants in the androgen receptor (AR) gene, and no replicated human genetic evidence implicates DAAM2 in its pathogenesis. DAAM2 (Dishevelled-associated activator of morphogenesis 2) is primarily studied in Wnt/planar cell polarity signaling, oligodendrocyte differentiation/myelination, bone mineral density GWAS, and renal/nephrotic phenotypes, none of which are established AIS mechanisms. A modest allowance for "Hypothesized" is warranted because Wnt/PCP signaling participates in urogenital and genital tubercle development, and formins can interact with androgen-responsive cytoskeletal pathways, so a biologically plausible but indirect link could be argued in the literature on AR-negative 46,XY DSD candidate genes. Some probability is retained for "Existing" in case an exome/candidate-gene study of AR-mutation-negative AIS-like 46,XY DSD reported a DAAM2 variant, but I am not aware of such a report. Overall, the pairing appears most consistent with "Novel."

NALCN encodes the voltage-independent sodium leak channel that sets neuronal resting membrane potential and controls excitability, so a biologically plausible link to seizure disorders exists; rodent and Drosophila (narrow abdomen) models and expression studies of leak conductance in hippocampal circuits support a hypothesized mechanistic role. In humans, NALCN variants are firmly linked to IHPRF1 (biallelic) and CLIFAHDD (de novo heterozygous) syndromes, in which seizures are an occasional but non-specific feature; none of these reports define temporal lobe epilepsy as the phenotype. I am not aware of replicated human genetic studies implicating NALCN specifically in temporal lobe epilepsy, either familial or sporadic, nor of significant common-variant associations in TLE GWAS. Some points remain for "Existing" because scattered epilepsy cohort/panel sequencing reports and syndromic patients with focal seizures could be interpreted as limited human evidence. "Established" is very unlikely, and "Novel" retains meaningful weight since the connection may be purely incidental beyond generic excitability biology.

Bent bone dysplasia syndrome type 1 is caused by FGFR2 mutations, and a distinct second form (BBDS-2, OMIM ~620076) has been attributed to biallelic LAMA5 variants, reported in human patients/fetuses with prenatally detected bent long bones, craniofacial anomalies and poor mineralization. LAMA5 encodes laminin alpha-5, a basement membrane component with well-documented roles in skeletal, craniofacial and renal development, and Lama5-null mice show skeletal/limb and placental defects, providing strong supportive biology. However, the human genetic evidence appears limited to one or a small number of consanguineous families/case reports rather than multiple independent replicated cohorts, so "Existing" is the most probable category, with meaningful weight on "Established" given the formal OMIM phenotype designation. Some probability remains for "Hypothesized" if the causal claim rests largely on functional/animal data plus a single family. "Novel" is very unlikely given the disorder is specifically named for this gene association.

ADCY1 lies within the DFNB44 linkage interval on chromosome 7p, and Santos-Cortez et al. (2014, Hum Mol Genet) reported a homozygous ADCY1 variant segregating with autosomal recessive nonsyndromic hearing impairment in a consanguineous Pakistani family, supported by zebrafish hair-cell/startle-response functional data. This constitutes credible human genetic evidence, but it rests essentially on a single family with little independent replication in subsequent cohorts. ClinGen-style curations of hearing loss genes have generally rated ADCY1 as limited (not definitive), and much of the supporting mechanistic evidence is from animal/in vitro work (cAMP signaling in hair cells), which would only support "Hypothesized." Therefore the weight falls on "Existing," with modest probability for "Established" and a meaningful residual for "Hypothesized" should the single human report be discounted.

SLIRP encodes a small RNA-binding protein that partners with LRPPRC to stabilize and polyadenylate mitochondrial mRNAs; LRPPRC biallelic variants are an established cause of French-Canadian Leigh syndrome, making SLIRP a strong biological candidate for combined OXPHOS deficiency. Robust functional support exists from Slirp knockout mice and cellular knockdown studies showing reduced mt-mRNA steady-state levels and impaired mitochondrial translation, which firmly supports at least the "Hypothesized" tier. I have a partial recollection of recent reports (within the last few years) describing biallelic SLIRP variants in patients with mitochondrial disease/combined OXPHOS deficiency, which would move the evidence into "Existing," but I am not confident this is replicated across multiple independent probands and rigorously validated. Given the very limited number of human cases reported to date, "Established" is unlikely, and "Novel" is essentially excluded by the strong mechanistic and animal-model data.

PPCDC (phosphopantothenoylcysteine decarboxylase) catalyzes the step immediately downstream of PPCS in the coenzyme A biosynthetic pathway, and biallelic PPCS variants are a proven cause of pediatric dilated cardiomyopathy (Iuso et al., AJHG 2018); other CoA pathway genes (PANK2, COASY) cause neurodegenerative/multisystem disease, making a strong biological and pathway-based rationale for PPCDC involvement in DCM. This pathway logic, together with CoA-deficiency models showing cardiac and metabolic consequences, supports at least a "Hypothesized" relationship. There may be isolated case reports or candidate variants in PPCDC identified in cardiomyopathy exome cohorts, which would justify "Existing," but I am not confident such human genetic evidence is firmly published or replicated. There is no robust, replicated human evidence establishing PPCDC as a DCM gene, so "Established" receives minimal weight, and "Novel" retains some probability in case the gene has never been implicated beyond incidental pathway membership.

VPS50 (CCDC132/syndetin), a subunit of the EARP endosomal recycling complex, has an established human disease association with a bi-allelic neurodevelopmental disorder (severe developmental delay, epilepsy, microcephaly, neonatal cholestasis; Schneeberger et al., AJHG 2021), but hydrocephalus is not a reported core feature of that phenotype. Some reported patients have nonspecific brain MRI findings such as corpus callosum abnormalities or mild ventriculomegaly, which could be interpreted as weak, indirect human evidence, but ventriculomegaly in this context is more likely atrophic/ex-vacuo than true hydrocephalus. Mechanistically, endosomal trafficking and vesicle recycling defects are plausibly relevant to ependymal/ciliary and CSF-flow biology, and rodent Vps50 models show neurodevelopmental abnormalities, supporting a hypothesized biological link rather than a demonstrated genetic one. Well-validated human hydrocephalus genes (L1CAM, MPDZ, CCDC88C, TRIM71, SMARCC1, FOXJ1) do not include VPS50, and I am unaware of replicated proband-level evidence tying VPS50 variants to hydrocephalus. Therefore probability mass is concentrated on Hypothesized and Novel, with modest weight on Existing.
